issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette:
John, a 56-year-old combat pilot, has spent three decades mastering the knife-edge of controlled risk. His life has been a testament to precision, discipline, and an unwavering belief in his ability to command his aircraft and his environment. Six months ago, that belief was shattered. During a routine training flight, a catastrophic engine failure triggered a violent explosion that tore through the fuselage. The cockpit filled with acrid smoke as alarms screamed, the jet pitching into an uncontrolled spin. The G-forces induced a sickening vertigo, and in the disorienting chaos of the ejection, he felt a profound sense of powerlessness he had never known. He landed hard, the impact fracturing his leg, and lay waiting for rescue, waves of nausea and dizziness washing over him as the wreck burned nearby.

The weeks that followed were a blur of hospitals and physical therapy, environments he came to associate with that initial, terrifying loss of control. He complied with treatment but felt a growing dread with each physical examination. Back at home, the world outside his window began to feel menacing. The sharp bang of a neighbour’s construction work would send a jolt of raw adrenaline through him, his body tensing as if for an imminent impact. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, his senses on high alert for any sudden movement or unexpected sound. This pervasive sense of threat was exhausting. To manage it, John began to shrink his world. He gave up his weekly golf game, unable to relax, startled into a defensive crouch by the sudden crack of a driver hitting a ball. The feeling of his body being constantly on guard made any attempt at leisure feel like a dangerous lapse in vigilance, so he simply stopped trying.

This self-imposed isolation has hollowed him out. The man who once commanded the skies now rarely leaves his house. He described to his wife a profound numbness, a feeling of being an observer to his own life, as if he were "dead inside." The core beliefs that had structured his identity—that skill mitigates risk, that the world operates on predictable principles—have been completely destroyed. In their place is a new, terrifying conviction: the world is a dangerous, random place, and disaster is always imminent. This new worldview has, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to his own body. Because he believes he is fundamentally unsafe, any fleeting internal sensation becomes a harbinger of catastrophe. A moment of lightheadedness from standing up too quickly is no longer benign; for John, it is the onset of another system failure, a sign that his own body is about to betray him just as his aircraft did.

This fear has driven him to seek control in the few domains he has left. He began to restrict his eating with military precision, believing that by managing his diet, he could prevent any internal feelings of illness or dizziness that might trigger his panic. Ironically, the strict caloric limits sometimes leave him feeling lightheaded, activating the very sensation he fears. As this cycle has tightened, his avoidance has intensified. The thought of his upcoming annual flight physical fills him with a dread so profound it feels physical. The memory of the post-crash hospital stay, of feeling ill and dizzy while doctors assessed him, merges with his current fear. Any minor feeling of being unwell now triggers an overwhelming urge to cancel the appointment and hide. His constant physical tension only reinforces this impulse; he is certain that submitting to an exam while his body is already primed for danger would be an unbearable ordeal.

John finally sought therapy after confessing to his wife that he was planning to feign an illness to avoid the physical, an act of deception that would effectively end the career that has defined his entire adult life. He is caught between the terror of losing his identity as a pilot and the even greater terror of the internal chaos that now governs his days. His hope is not just to fly again, but to feel solid ground beneath his feet, to live in a world that does not feel like it is perpetually on the verge of falling apart.
